title: Chrome for journalists on Mac: tabs, archives, and reporting tips with Lazur
metaTitle: Chrome for Journalists on Mac: Tabs, Archives, and Lazur
description: Chrome for journalists on Mac: tab groups, Tab Search, archive checks and reading tips. Plus how Lazur answers questions about your page out loud.
secondaryKeywords: archive web pages in chrome on mac
voice assistant for chrome on mac
intro: Chrome on a Mac already covers most of the browser side of reporting. You get tab groups, Tab Search, reopened tabs, and history that syncs when you sign in. Lazur adds a voice on top: hold ⌥ ⌘, ask about the page in front of you, and hear the answer out loud.
tldr: Make one tab group per story, and check the sync effect before you delete a group.
Archive every page you plan to cite, and write the date you saved it next to the link.
Check your newsroom's AI rules before you use Gemini in Chrome on a draft or a leaked document.
Hold ⌥ ⌘ in Chrome to ask Lazur about the page. It answers out loud and can circle a control.
The survey numbers here come from a 2016 study of small-market newspapers. Read them as a snapshot, not a census.

blocks.text: Most reporting in Chrome means many open tabs, long pages, and sources that change or disappear. Chrome has a built-in answer for most of those problems. The trick is to set it up on a quiet afternoon, not in the middle of a deadline.
Set up Chrome on your Mac for reporting before a deadline

Start with a profile. If you also use Chrome for personal browsing, make a separate profile for reporting. Click the profile icon at the top right of the window and choose Add. Bookmarks, history, and tab groups stay inside that profile, so your personal logins and your source list do not mix.

Next, check the version. Choose Chrome > About Google Chrome from the menu bar. Google's Chrome Enterprise release notes list Chrome 152 with a stable date of September 1, 2026, and Chrome 151 on August 7, 2026. The Chrome Releases blog posted an Early Stable desktop update on November 4, 2026, but that post does not show a version number. Restart Chrome after an update so it takes effect.

blocks.title: Check sync first
blocks.text: Tab groups save and sync across devices when your browsing history and tabs sync with your Google Account. Before you build a story around a group, confirm which profile and account you are signed in to.
Group tabs by story so the window stays readable

A tab group is a named, colored set of tabs. Google's help page describes the steps for adding a tab. Right-click a tab, choose Add tab to group, then choose New group or an existing group. Use one group for each story, and name it after the story, not the day.

items: Right-click the first tab you need for the story.
Choose Add tab to group, then New group.
Type a short name, such as the council budget or a case number, and pick a color.
Right-click each other tab, choose Add tab to group, and pick the group.
Click the group name or the colored circle to collapse it. Click again to expand.

blocks.text: Multi-select is where Mac users get stuck. Google's help page tells you to hold Ctrl and click each tab. It does not give the Mac version. On a Mac, Ctrl-click usually opens the right-click menu, so test ⌘-click on two tabs before you rely on it. If it does not work, add tabs one at a time.

Take a city council story. Your group might hold the agenda, the minutes, the budget PDF, a few of your earlier articles on the project, and the state records search. Collapse the group while you write the draft. Expand it when you need the agenda again. The window stays short, and the sources stay together.

blocks.title: Deleting syncs too
blocks.text: Deleting a group, or ungrouping its tabs, also removes the group on other devices that use the same account. Copy your source list into a doc before you clean up a finished story.
Tab Search and keyboard shortcuts for faster switching

Tab Search finds a tab you cannot see. On a Mac, press ⌘⇧A, type a few words from the page title, and pick the match. This beats scanning a crowded strip, especially when several tabs come from the same publisher.

blocks.caption: Shortcuts and menu items from Google's Chrome tab help page.

blocks.text: Vertical tabs help when titles are long. Choose View > Show Tabs Vertically, and the tabs stack down the side of the window. Long headlines and document names stay readable. Use the same menu to switch back when you want the wide strip.

Reopening is a common fix and a common trap. ⌘⇧T brings back the last tab you closed. Press it again to bring back the one before that. For a page you closed days ago, skip the shortcut, open Chrome > History, and search by site or title.
Archive a page before you cite it

Web pages change. A press release gets edited after it goes out. A county page moves to a new address. Save a copy when you find the page, not after your story runs. A public archive gives you a dated copy you can point to if the original changes.

The Wayback Checker Chrome extension checks whether the current page is archived on the Wayback Machine and archive.today. It can save a snapshot right away, and it shows up to five recent snapshots for a site. It is a convenience tool. It is not a newsroom standard.

blocks.title: Low adoption
blocks.text: The Chrome Web Store listing shows 13 users and no ratings, and the developer is an individual. Read the permissions before you install it, and check your newsroom's list of approved extensions.

items: Copy the page address from the address bar.
Save the page in the Wayback Machine, or use an archive checker you trust.
Paste the snapshot link into your notes beside the quote.
Write the date you saved it. Pages change after you read them.

blocks.text: Read paywalled and gated sources the right way

Paywalls slow reporters down, and a blocked page can make a strong source look thin. Start with your newsroom's own subscriptions and any library account you have. If the source is a government body or a company, ask the press office to send the document.

Do not use tricks to get past a paywall. They can break a site's terms of use, and a copy you got that way is hard to defend in a correction. Keep the PDF in a folder with a clear name, and note the page number of every quote.
Use Gemini in Chrome without sending the wrong page

Chrome includes Gemini. MakeUseOf says that when you click Ask Gemini, Gemini automatically sees the page you are viewing. Before you click it on an unpublished draft, a leaked memo, or a page with a source's private details, check your newsroom's AI rules.
Gemini in Chrome can be disabled. If your newsroom has no AI policy yet, turn it off on a work Mac until someone writes one. You can switch it back on later.

The shortcut for the Gemini floating window is not settled. MakeUseOf says Ctrl+G opens it on a Mac, and Ctrl+Shift+G starts content selection. Other sources give Command+G for the same job. Check Chrome's own menus before you build a habit around a key.

Lazur listens differently. You hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask, and Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models.
A worked example: from first tab to cited quote
Here is a records story from start to finish. It shows where each Chrome tool fits, and where a mistake usually happens.

items: Search for the agency page and open it. Put it in a new group named for the records request.
Save an archived copy of the page the moment you find the data table.
Download the PDF to a folder named for the story. Rename it with the date it was published.
Open a notes doc. For each quote, paste the URL, the page or line number, and the date you read it.
Ask Lazur to explain a dense table, then check its answer against the source before you use a number.
Draft the paragraph in your doc. Dictate the rough sentences with fn, then edit by hand.

blocks.text: A common mistake is skipping the archive step. You find the table, read it, and move on. The page changes two weeks later, and the only copy of the number is in your memory. Save first, then read.
Edge cases on a shared Mac and a sensitive story

A shared Mac changes the rules. Sign out of Chrome when you finish, and check which profile is open before you type a source's name. A newsroom laptop that moves between desks needs the same care as a personal one.

Lazur keeps a memory of what you asked and did, and that memory stays on the Mac. On a sensitive story, think about what that memory holds before you lend the Mac to someone else. Treat it like your notes, not like scratch paper.
Watch for copies that look like the original. A repost of a press release can be wrong, and the date may be missing. Check the original site before you cite a copy.
What the survey data says about reporters' time

Few studies measure how reporters use browsers. The most direct source here is a Tow Center survey fielded online from November 14 to December 4, 2016. It received 420 eligible responses from small-market newspaper journalists. Its authors say it is self-selecting and not representative.

Read those numbers with care. The respondents worked at small papers, and the survey is from 2016. Still, the findings point to two themes. Workload is high, and most people learn their tools on their own. One respondent wrote: 'The biggest challenge facing small-market newspapers is manpower and time.'

Muck Rack's State of Journalism 2026 page says its survey covers more than 1,000 journalists. It asks where they spend their time and how they use AI. The page does not publish tool or time percentages, so this page does not quote any from it.

One number often gets mixed up with reporter data. A 2019 Medill/Spiegel Research Center study found that desktop visitors to three newspaper sites spent under 1% of their internet time on those sites. That study measures readers, not journalists. Use it to think about audiences, not to judge your own tab habits.
Where Lazur fits in a Chrome session

Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac that lives in the notch. Hold ⌥ ⌘ and ask about anything on screen. It answers out loud. Ask where something is, and it draws a circle and a label around it. Ask how to do something, and it guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click.
Lazur does not click buttons, edit files, or operate other apps for you. It is not a plugin or add-in for any app. It has no partnership with any app maker, Chrome included.

The research feature runs in Lazur's own Chrome tabs, through the Lazur for Chrome extension. It comes back with a summary and a report. Your working tabs stay where you left them. That helps when you need background on a company while you keep writing.

A simple test for your first session: open a dense page, hold ⌥ ⌘, and ask Lazur to explain the section you are stuck on. Then ask where Tab Search is. The answer comes out loud, and the circle shows you the control. Ask for a walkthrough when a step is unfamiliar.
Mistakes that waste a reporting afternoon

items: Deleting a tab group on one Mac, which removes it on other devices that share the account.
Trusting an archive link with no date. Write the date you saved it next to the link.
Clicking Ask Gemini on a draft before your newsroom has a rule for AI.
Using Ctrl-click when you want multi-select on a Mac. Test ⌘-click first.
Treating an extension with a small user count as approved. Check permissions and your newsroom's list.

blocks.text: Lazur trial and plans for reporters

Lazur is a Mac app with a free trial that needs no credit card. The trial starts when you first open the app. Plans are Pro and Power, and dictation is unlimited on both. Check the pricing page for current plans and how many AI actions each one includes.
A setup checklist for your next story

items: Open a reporting profile, and confirm which account you are signed in to.
Check Chrome > About Google Chrome against Google's release notes.
Group tabs by story, and name each group for the story.
Set up Tab Search with ⌘⇧A, and turn on vertical tabs if titles get cut off.
Archive every page you will cite, and write the date next to it.
Hold ⌥ ⌘ when you need a page explained, and ask Lazur for a walkthrough when you need a button.

blocks.text: Start with one story. Set up the group and the archive habit first, then add the rest of the tools as you need them.

faq.question: Can I group tabs in Chrome on a Mac?
faq.answer: Yes. Right-click a tab, choose Add tab to group, then choose New group or an existing group. Click the group name or the colored circle to collapse it. Groups sync across devices when your tabs and history sync with your Google Account.

faq.question: What is the Tab Search shortcut in Chrome on a Mac?
faq.answer: Press ⌘⇧A. Google's Chrome tab help page lists it. Type part of a page title to find the tab, then select the match.

faq.question: How do I reopen a tab I closed by mistake?
faq.answer: Press ⌘⇧T. Each press reopens the next most recently closed tab. For a page you closed a while ago, open Chrome > History and search by site or title.

faq.question: Is Lazur a Chrome extension?
faq.answer: No. Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. Its research feature runs in Lazur's own Chrome tabs through the Lazur for Chrome extension. Lazur is not a plugin or add-in for any app.

faq.question: Can Lazur click buttons in Chrome for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur does not click buttons, edit files, or operate other apps for you. It draws a circle and a label around a control, and it guides you one click at a time while waiting for each click.

faq.question: Does Lazur work on Windows?
faq.answer: Not yet. Lazur runs on macOS, on Apple silicon and Intel Macs. Windows is planned, not available.

faq.question: Does Lazur send my screen somewhere?
faq.answer: Lazur listens and looks at the screen only while you hold the shortcut. Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer, and they are not stored. Content is never used to train AI models. Still check your newsroom rules before you ask about an unpublished draft.

faq.question: Is the Wayback Checker extension safe to use?
faq.answer: The Chrome Web Store listing shows 13 users and no ratings, and the developer is an individual. That is not enough to vouch for it. Read its permissions, and check your newsroom's approved list before you install it.

faq.question: How much does Lazur cost after the trial?
faq.answer: Lazur has two paid plans, Pro and Power. The current prices and AI action limits are on the pricing page. Dictation is unlimited on both plans.
